query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated damage arises because mechanical wear continuously ruptures the protective oxide/passive layer on the more reactive intermetallic (e.g., B2 or σ) phases, exposing fresh surfaces in each contact cycle, which drives localized galvanic corrosion at elevated temperatures and thus amplifies total mass loss compared to purely wear or corrosion alone.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or as-clad multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based system) with distinct soft and hard phases (FCC, B2, Laves, or σ phases) and initial protective oxide scale formed by high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Subjection of the alloy to sliding or abrasive contact in a corrosive environment under elevated temperature (around 600 °C), controlling mechanical load and chemical conditions to allow oxide layer formation and rupture during wear-corrosion cycling.
generation.conditions: Tribo-corrosion environment: elevated temperature (~600 °C), corrosive solution (e.g., chloride or acidic molten salt), with precisely tuned normal loads and sliding speeds. Electrochemical conditions monitored via polarization tests during wear to track real-time corrosion response.
generation.structural_mediator: Microgalvanic couples formed by compositionally distinct phases (e.g., B2, σ, or Laves with different electrochemical potentials) in the eutectic microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The repeated removal of the oxide/passivation film by mechanical action reveals freshly exposed surfaces on phases with distinct corrosion susceptibilities, creating localized galvanic cells. This intensifies electrochemical dissolution, weakens the matrix–intermetallic interfaces, and results in accelerated material removal (both wear and corrosion) beyond the sum of the isolated processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline test without simultaneous abrasion or without elevated temperature, total mass loss will be significantly higher in the tribo-corrosion condition. Individually, corrosion current density and wear rate both increase under simultaneous wear-corrosion relative to their single-mode levels, but the combined total degradation is disproportionally larger (i.e., super-additive).
generation.baseline: Separate measurements of pure corrosion (no mechanical load) and pure wear (in inert or dry environment) carried out at the same temperature, used to compare against the degradation behavior observed under tribo-corrosion exposure.
generation.boundary: Above a critical temperature (near 400–600 °C), oxide/passive films form but are more easily disrupted by mechanical contact. Below this temperature or in a non-aggressive environment, synergy is diminished. Alloys with single-phase or more uniform microstructures may not exhibit the same degree of accelerated damage.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in oxide stability and local electrochemical potentials among various high-entropy alloy compositions remain unclear and may shift the temperature threshold or the relative magnitude of the wear vs. corrosion contribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tribo-corrosion tests on multi-phase eutectic HEA samples under systematically varied mechanical loads and temperatures (e.g., 400 °C vs. 600 °C) in a chloride or molten salt environment. Compare total mass loss and surface damage morphology for tests with and without mechanical rubbing at each temperature.
measurements: Real-time friction coefficient and wear rate
Potentiodynamic polarization scans and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy during wear
Post-exposure microstructural characterization of oxide films, corrosion morphologies, and phase-specific dissolution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant increase in total degradation (mass loss or morphological signs of synergy) is observed in simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions compared to the sum of separate wear and corrosion tests, then the hypothesized mechanism of oxide disruption–driven galvanic synergy is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

Degradation of materials under various operating conditions, especially in corrosive flow environments, can seriously affect the durability of the components []. During use, components are required to withstand various forms of degradation, such as cavitation, abrasive wear, and corrosion. In turn, flow machine components such as pipelines, valves, rotors, and turbines are severely exposed to various forms of deterioration, such as slurry erosion, cavitation, and degradation under corrosive conditions, which intensify their deterioration process []. The problems associated with various wear processes require high corrosion resistance from the materials in addition to favorable mechanical properties. Among engineers, stainless steels have so far been the first choice for applications in aggressive corrosive environments []. The recent interest in HEAs (high-entropy alloys) may provide an alternative for use in corrosion-resistant steels []. Although the corrosion resistance of stainless steels is at an acceptable level, they have relatively limited and sometimes insufficient mechanical properties []. FeCoNiCuAl high-entropy alloys exhibit remarkable mechanical properties; nevertheless, these materials struggle to withstand harsh environments because of their insufficient resistance to wear and corrosion. The addition of Si can significantly enhance the alloy’s high-temperature performance, hardness, and wear resistance, thereby making it more suitable for applications in high-temperature or corrosive environments. To overcome these drawbacks, this research investigates how varying Si content affects the microstructure and properties of FeCoNiCuAl coatings. Composite coatings of FeCoNiCuAlSix (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0) were fabricated on 65 Mn substrates using laser cladding. Various testing methods, including metallographic microscopy, Vickers hardness testing, friction and wear testing, and electrochemical analysis, were employed to examine the phase structure, microstructure, and hardness of the coating.
